en: The Illustrated Scripture on the Establishment of the Precept Platform in Guanzhong, with Preface.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Shi Daoxuan of Ximing Monastery in the Capital of the Great Tang.

Preface: I, being of dull and obscure intellect, participated in the academies for learning during my youth. I cultivated myself in the meaning of the teachings and consulted with the wise and enlightened, seeking their instruction.

The Way was severed from the Confucian classics; only by revering virtue and upholding the establishment of the Way could one dwell without a fixed teacher, pursuing a thousand li as if it were but a few inches.
Devoting oneself solely to the Dharma, one crosses the passes and rivers as if over a single reed.
Wandering through the regions of Jin and Wei, he had repeatedly consulted and read [the texts] since his first hearing of them;
surveying the lands of Jiang and Huai, he had gained insights through the casual conversations of the road.

Thus, at the age of twenty, he began to seek out the ink and lead [of the scriptures]. Regarding the essentials of the Vinaya, the conduct of practice, and strategic deliberations, his commentaries and diagrams became prominent in the minds of his contemporaries, while his abridgments and sub-commentaries opened the way for those with discernment. Whether providing annotations or exegesis, his citations were drawn from the preceding scriptures.
At times suppressing and at times elevating, the focus lies solely on accomplishing practical tasks.

While the immediate circumstances are fully addressed, the gradual evolution of the tradition can be discerned; yet as for the fundamental precepts and the ritual grounds, they have never been set forth in detail. Although these matters are recounted according to specific events, they ultimately do not constitute erroneous statements.

This year, my mind has been unrestrained; like the *púliǔ* tree, I may fall at any moment. Having sought this path, I feel as if I were falling into a moat; thus, I have written this with all my failing strength. That it remains incomplete is no fault of mine. It was in the second year of the Qiánfēng era that I began to propagate this Dharma in the southern suburbs of the capital.
Originally, the establishment of the *śīla-maṇḍala* was for the purpose of instituting the precepts.
The precepts are the fundamental basis of conduct for all sages and the life-root of the Three Dharmas;
through them, the Supreme Awakening gives rise to compassion, and by means of them, ordinary delusions are brought to extinction.
Therefore, the text says:
"How is it known that the Buddha-dharma will endure for a long time?
If there are ten people in the central lands or five people in the border regions who receive the precepts according to the Dharma, this is called the long endurance of the True Dharma."
Thus we know that the deportment of a bhikṣu does not exist apart from the precepts; the Way must be propagated by persons, and it cannot be established without the precepts.

The precepts are realized through the performance of ritual acts, and such acts necessarily arise depending upon a specific site. This site is called the "Precept Platform" (Jietan); ascending and descending it causes the mind to become inspired and transcendent. The ground is designated as supremely virtuous;
when the boundary is formally established through chanting, the ritual application becomes earnest and diligent.
Is it not because extraordinary rituals can move toward extraordinary ends?
Thus, if one examines their breadth, discussions may be settled therein;
yet if one seeks their essence, actual practice is difficult to take as a standard.
Therefore, various Vinaya texts state:

"The boundary markers are neglected regarding their limits; the proclamations are confused regarding prior conditions; the assembled community does not understand distinctions between the different and the same; and the general harmony is muddled regarding success and failure."
They replied together:
"Since it does not belong to any realm and entirely deviates from the principles of the sages, although one may receive it, one cannot obtain its fruit because there is no realm.
Thus we know:
To construct a building on empty ground is merely to waste effort and achieve nothing; without an altar and the delimitation of boundaries (*sīmābandha*), the victorious mind is difficult to arouse.

Now, having extensively searched through various records and synthesized all that I have heard, I open this initial gate for the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*), looking up to the bequeathed rules of those who dwell in the Dharma.

If the various methods were not categorized, those who calculate through推算 (tuī bù) would not understand their origins; therefore, I have briefly established these various sections so that those of keen intellect may know they are not arbitrarily devised.
The First Section on the Founding of the Teaching and the Establishment of the Altar Site:
Originally, it was solely the Buddha who presided over the assembly from the ten directions; he detailed the altar site in full, as first discussed during the time of Tathāgata King of Radiance.
Therefore, its establishment depends on the Great Sage and not on human deliberation; this is the height of reverence.

Regarding the second point, the formal naming and manifest title of the *kṣetraguṇa* (precept platform), a thorough examination of the Vinaya and Śāstras reveals that they frequently refer to it simply as the "Precept Platform" (*jietan*).

In the customs of the time, these were conflated such that the *tán* and the *chǎng* could not be distinguished; thus, various records cite them interchangeably, with name and reality both running amok. Is this not merely a matter of long-standing habit, where clinging to the stump makes reform difficult?

Section Three: The Form and Characteristics of the Precept Platform. Since it is called a "platform" (*maṇḍala*), it rises from the ground as a tiered foundation; its form is like that of the King of Mountains (*Sumeru*), and its appearance is identical to the seat of the Buddha.
The steps are arranged in four tiers, encircling three levels; the sacred relics serve as a guardian to ensure the flourishing of the Dharma.
Regarding the height, depth, width, and breadth of the precept platform, the fourth tier’s measurements are fixed according to the Buddha’s cubit;
as for its overall dimensions, these are determined by circumstances and adapted to the capacity of the practitioners.
There is no fixed limit to its size; it emerges from the deliberations and universal principles of the wise.
Regarding the fifth section on the comprehensive details of the precept platform (*śīlakaṇḍa*) and the inner and outer boundaries (*sīmā*), this explains the conditions for being inside or outside.
Now, seeking the matter through principle, the external intention is distinct.

Regarding the sequence of the ritual for establishing the *śīlā-sthāna* (precept platform), according to the sixth [section] on the practices of ancient virtuous masters, the *mahā-sīmā* (great boundary) comes first.
Now, preserving this for clear inspection, the platform precedes and the boundary follows.

Regarding the assembly of the Sangha at the ordination platform, the seventh boundary (sīmā) must be established first. As for the initial laying of the foundation and the ritual procedures for assembling the monks, there are already established regulations.
Later students who follow their own inclinations often neglect their fundamental duties; they must instead focus intently on the scriptural net and assemble people according to the Dharma.

Chapter Eight: The Success or Failure of the Ritual Procedures for the Precept Platform (*Sīmaṇḍala-karman*). “Karma” is the term in the Western language; in the Tang language, it is called “performing the ritual action” (*jizuò*).
Its meaning requires a discernment of success and failure, as well as a clear understanding of the temporal conditions.
Regarding the term "Sangha," it signifies that the six harmonies are not in discord; regarding the description of "matters," it means that the four boundaries each encompass their respective domains.

The ninth section on the ritual for receiving [the precepts] at a *śīlakaṇḍa* (precept altar) refers to the procedural rules for ordination, which have been transmitted from antiquity to the present; if the altar is omitted, the ascent and descent will lose their proper order.
Therefore, the Sages established models so that teachers and disciples might maintain proper decorum; their circumambulations, prostrations, and standing were like the movement of a loom’s shuttle.
Regarding the eleventh [topic], the efficacy of the Precept Platform: once the Sangha has completed the ordination, it endures for sixty thousand years.
Even when the Three Dharmas perish, this site remains constant through the succession of thousands of sages, and is thus called the "Vajra Ground."
The significance of these names is such that none but the Sages can fully comprehend them; ordinary people may only look up to them with reverence and must not treat them with contempt.

Chapter Eleven: Praising the Virtues of the Precept Platform. The supreme virtues of the precept platform are followed by all the Sages. It is here that one establishes unsurpassed roots of goodness and eradicates the profound karmic burdens of the most debased state. One must surely pass through this ground before one can attain the highest honor.
Is it not to commemorate divine feats and extol sacred virtue?
First, regarding the Origin and Establishment of the Precept Platform by Yuan Jie: The first section, based on the *Biexuan*, states:
"When the Buddha was at the Jeta Grove, the bhikṣu Lohitaka requested the Buddha to establish a platform for the purpose of binding precepts and conferring ordination."
At that time, the Tathāgata, having granted his consent as requested, established three altars for the first time:

the one to the east of the Buddha Hall gate was named "The Altar Where the Buddha Established the Precepts for Bhikṣus," and the one to the west of the Buddha Hall gate was named "The Altar Where the Buddha Established the Precepts for Bhikṣuṇīs."
To the south of the eastern gate of the outer courtyard, the "Sangha Ordination Platform for Bhikṣus" was established.
On the day the platform was first established, the Buddhas of the ten directions were assembled; at that time, there were eight hundred billion Buddhas, all sharing the same name, Śākyamuni Buddha.
Among the Buddhas of the ten directions, those with the same names were likewise as numerous.
At that time, Mahābrahmādeva constructed the eastern ordination platform within the Buddha’s courtyard, and Māra Pāpīyas constructed the western ordination platform within the Buddha’s courtyard.
Once the platforms were completed, the Buddhas ascended them.

They deliberated together on the characteristics of the gravity of the precepts, their observance and violation, and so forth; they further discussed the matter of ordaining nuns and how it would lead to the extinction of the True Dharma.
All the Buddhas deliberated in unison, saying:
"In antiquity there were four assemblies; why is it that now there are none alone?"
Although the True Dharma was originally destined to perish after half its duration, because they were able to practice the Eight Respectful Observances, it remained for another thousand years.
Therefore, these two altars are ascended by the Buddha alone, as they share in the magnitude of his enlightened activities.

The Sangha’s ordination platform is not included within the category of the Sangha; when there are occasions where a holy person is ordained, they also attend the Sangha platform, performing the ritual at that time, yet it is not subsumed under formal *karmavācanā*.

2. Establishing the Name and Manifesting the Title of the Precept Platform (Śīlamaṇḍala). Section Two. Regarding the distinction between "field" (*kṣetra*) and "platform" (*maṇḍala*) as revealed in the Vinaya treatises: while various kingdoms in the Western Heavens all establish distinct rituals for these, it is not to be wondered at that such practices were originally never performed in the Central Plains of this land.
Now that its name and reality have been definitively established, there may be differing opinions.
According to the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Sengzhuan*), it states:

"During the Yuanjia era of Emperor Wen of the Song dynasty, the holy monk Guṇavarman traveled to Jianye for the purpose of proselytization. He erected a precept platform in the garden in front of Nanlin Temple, ordering those receiving the precepts to ascend the platform to receive them."
"After his passing, he was further cremated upon the altar.
The remainder is as cited below.
Furthermore, Kumāralāta, the master who translated the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, in his *Answers to the Five Hundred Questions*, also stated regarding Dharma Master Huiguan:
"The master on the platform bestows the precepts upon others.
The remainder of the text is extensive and will not be recounted here.
Thus, we know that the name "platform" (tán) has been in use for a long time.
People today do not recognize this; they blur the distinctions and follow one another blindly, failing to differentiate between the level ground and the high altar.
How mistaken!
According to the *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography), it says:

"After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, when Kāśyapa convened the council at the precept platform, he had the junior Maudgalyāyana strike the bell to summon the assembly of ordinary and noble monks from ten billion four-continent worlds."

Once the assembly had gathered at the altar, the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* was performed. After the punishment for the offenses of Piṇḍola and Ānanda was concluded, Ānanda was instructed to don the Buddha’s saṃghāṭī robe and take his seat as the presiding elder. He then recited the *Śāstradāna Sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching) according to the Buddha’s injunctions; thereupon, the great bodhisattvas, arhats, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas all wept with great compassion.

Mahākāśyapa rose from his seat, donned his coarse *saṃghāṭī* robe, and took up his *niṣīdana*. He went before Ānanda, spread out his *niṣīdana*, and after paying homage to Ānanda, circumambulated him three times to the right.

Mahābrahmā held a great precious parasol over Ānanda’s head; Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, advanced with a table of the seven treasures and placed it before Ānanda; Māra Pāpīyas brought a fly-whisk of the seven treasures and presented it to Ānanda. Māra and Śakra attended on both sides, while the Four Heavenly Kings stood in attendance at the four legs of the high seat. The thirty-two messengers followed behind Kāśyapa, kneeling alternately.
Having prostrated, Kāśyapa approached Ānanda and inquired after his well-being; his manner was no different from when the World-Honored One was still present.
At that time, Kāśyapa posed three thousand eight hundred questions on various matters of doubt, and Ānanda answered each one of them.
Now, I shall briefly extract one question concerning the *śīlā-maṇḍala* (precept altar), omitting the rest.
Mahākāśyapa asked:
"In the twenty years since you followed the Tathāgata, what cubit measurement did you rely upon for the height, depth, width, and breadth of the precept altar?"
Are śarīra relics enshrined within the center of the ordination platform?
What materials are used to pave the four sides of the ordination platform?
How many steps are opened on each of the four sides, and by how much do they differ from one another?
"What forms and images should be made around the four sides of the altar?
In a country where there are no stones, should they be made of earth and sand?
Ānanda answered him exactly according to the illustrations in this scroll.
To the north of the original Jetavana Precept Platform was a bell tower four hundred feet high, topped with a golden bell weighing one hundred thousand catties, a rare and magnificent sight;
beneath it were images of nine coiling dragons, from whose mouths flowed water of eight meritorious qualities.

When the person seeking ordination arrived at the site of the altar, the dragon immediately spat forth water to drench his head, resembling the manner in which a Wheel-Turning King ascends the altar to receive his consecration.

Therefore, when a person first receives the precepts, it is as if they were receiving the rank of a Dharma King from the Buddha, the Dharma King. There is the light of a *maṇi* jewel which, upon touching the recipient of the precepts, brings them the bliss of purity; furthermore, it symbolizes that the recipient has received the pure jewel of the precepts.

When the noble ones receive the precepts, they obtain the power to strike the Bodhisattva bell; its sound shakes the trichiliocosm, such that those who hear it realize the fruits of enlightenment and the evil realms are brought to rest.

When an ordinary person receives [the blow], he causes the bhikṣu Madika to strike it, and the sound reaches a small thousand-world system; this bhikṣu possesses strength equal to that of one hundred thousand men.

The bell tower was shaped like Mount Sumeru and stood within a great pond; nine dragons thrust their heads upward, coiled together to support it, with all the beams and pillars resting upon these dragon heads, all fashioned of gold.

The roof tiles were made of crystal; if anyone ascended the altar to receive [the teachings], the dragons would immediately turn their course, emitting fragrant rain and fragrant clouds from their mouths, which covered and sprinkled the altar.
The four sides of the pond are paved with white jade, and its bottom is strewn with silver sand. The water is pure and clear, as sweet as milk or honey.
If those who uphold the precepts drink from it when ill, they will all be cured;
yet if those who have broken the precepts drink, it is like swallowing molten iron.
When the Buddha was about to enter *nirvāṇa*, the waters first dried up and the roof tiles flew away;

when Kāśyapa convened the council and Ānanda gave his responses, the roof tiles returned and the pond again produced water, white in color like milk, yet lacking the taste of milk. This symbolizes that after the [Buddha’s] passing, the True Dharma (*saddharma*) will likewise perish, becoming successively flavorless. This may be understood by reference to the analogy of adding water to milk found in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.

When the assembly’s questioning and compilation of the teachings were complete, the Sangha departed for the royal city. The great bell and the jeweled platform flew up to the Tuṣita Heaven; the jade of the pond and the silver sands were taken away by the Dragon King, and the water also dried up.

Now, although this site has no distinct physical characteristics whatsoever, because its original conditions were obscured, the altar site was established there; therefore, I shall describe it in detail.
The naming of the "altar" (tán) dates back to the time of the Buddha!

In this land, there currently exist numerous sūtras, vinayas, and śāstras, all of which clarify the circumstances of the two assemblies held in the royal city; yet, as their accounts differ in what they include or omit, this does not detract from Ānanda’s status as the primary master who ascended the throne to compile the Dharma.
Only the question posed by Kāśyapa remains: when Ānanda assumed a form identical to that of the Buddha, all the bhikṣus suspected he was the Buddha;
their doubts ceased only upon hearing the words, “Thus have I heard.”

Regarding what is transmitted today, those who have attained thorough realization do not perceive this land; even those who bind themselves to the characteristics of phenomena do not yet know it themselves. How much more so for those who appear now and lack faith—this is indeed to be expected.
From the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa through the periods of the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma, the manner in which the councils were convened has followed many paths.

First, there was the council of five hundred; next, that of one thousand; then, that of the Great Assembly; then, that of King Aśoka; and finally, that of seven hundred. These five instances are set forth here; though others certainly exist, those mentioned above all pertain to the Hīnayāna.

As for the Mahāyāna, Ānanda and Kāśyapa conducted an extensive compilation at the royal city, while Mañjuśrī and the great bodhisattvas conducted a concise compilation at Mount Cakravāḍa, as described in various sūtras of this land.
3. The Form and Characteristics of the Ordination Platform (Sīmā-maṇḍala). Section Three: Revealing the characteristics according to their names, there are distinct ritual procedures.
"Field" (*cháng*) refers to clearing the ground to make it pure, removing all mounds and hollows; this is what is meant by leveling the ground in common worldly practice!
Theatres and battlefields can be understood by analogy with this.

As for the characteristics of a "platform" (tán), it involves excavating the ground to establish a foundation; this refers to the various platforms used for sacrifices and rituals in the four suburbs.
In my inspection of the various altars, those with square bases are numerous.
Only the single altar of the Round Mound (Yuánqīu) has its base divided into nine sectors, each provided with steps and stairways; the reasons for this are as explained elsewhere.
The ordination platform of today was originally created by Heaven; its craftsmanship is so exquisite that its principles transcend human ingenuity.
Furthermore, as it was designed by the Buddha’s own direction, it is not within the scope of ordinary measures; thus, its features differ from those of common worldly custom.
According to the *Biézhuan*:

"The ordination platform rises from the ground, its form consisting of three tiers to symbolize the Three Emptinesses (*trīṇi śūnyatāni*). It serves as the initial gateway for entering the Buddha-dharma, dispersing and releasing the delusions of ordinary beings; nothing can dispel these but emptiness."

The three levels of emptiness are the dwelling places for those who have attained the Way, and right precepts serve as the foundation for all virtues; therefore, they are limited to these three layers!
Formerly, the Buddha Prabhāsa-rāja established the rule that the height should be five cubits (*hasta*) to symbolize the Dharma-body of fivefold qualities;
Śākyamuni Tathāgata reduced it to two and a half cubits.
Above this, he further added two inches to make three tiers;
subsequently, Śakra Devendra added a lid shaped like an inverted cauldron upon the altar to cover the śarīra,
and Mahābrahmā placed a priceless jewel atop the inverted cauldron-shaped lid as an offering to the śarīra.
This constitutes five tiers, which further represent the fivefold Dharma-body (pañcadharmakāya): the first tier is one cubit high; the second tier is two and a half cubits high;
the third tier is two inches high, which constitutes one-third [of the total height];
and with the addition of Śakra’s covering cauldron, it becomes four tiers.
When the Brahma King added a precious gem, there were five layers, thus completing the five parts.

When the Buddha was first in the world, after the ordination platform had been established within the Jetavana Garden, the precious gem bestowed by the Great Brahma King was as large as a five-sheng jar; those with great merit and virtue who beheld it saw its radiance illuminate eight hundred *yojanas*.
Those of meager merit see it as if it were a mass of ink.
Throughout the Tathāgata’s lifetime, it was always present at the ordination platform; when the Buddha entered nirvāṇa, the pearl likewise vanished along with him.
When the Venerable Mahākāśyapa was conducting the council, the pearl returned; when Ānanda entered parinirvāṇa, the pearl departed again.

Later, the Great Brahmā King took a bright pearl to replace it for the purpose of making offerings to the śarīra. Below the pearl, a jeweled lotus was used to support it, and nine dragons were fashioned to support the feet of the flower.

Śakra, Lord of Devas, further offered two jewels to venerate the śarīra, using golden lotuses as footstools and setting up golden pillars beneath them, with lion figures placed at the base of the pillars;
once the compilation was completed, these two jewels both vanished.
The two jewels of Śakra are currently in the Nandana Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where they make offerings to the Prajñāpāramitā.
At present, when altars are established in various places, if there are no jewels available for offering, one should provide two bright lamps according to one's ability.
Whether of stone or wood, these [structures] shall always stand before the altar, higher than the upper tier, so that their radiance shines afar and illuminates both above and below.
The ground upon the altar is paved with stone; whenever there is an occasion for receiving the precepts, a high seat is specially installed in the southwest corner so that the bhikṣu may ascend it.

Should the ascent be difficult or obstructed, at such times the Great Brahmā King, to the west of the western stairs on the southern side, manifests a silver lotus with an iron stem. Its petals open and close like a revolving mechanism, joined together so that they face the balustrade and correspond exactly with the high seat, ensuring that those who ascend meet no impediment.
"Since the Jetavana has been destroyed, this tradition has also ceased; nevertheless, those who would create [such works] hereafter may proceed according to this model.

Recently, in the ninth month of the second year of the Qianfeng era, the Venerable Śākyamitrā, a śramaṇa from the Mahābodhi Temple in Central India and a man of advanced age who had spent ninety-nine summer retreats in practice, came to Mount Wutai to pay his respects to Mañjuśrī.

The present Emperor treated him with great courtesy and ordered an envoy to escort him back; upon returning to the south of the suburbs, he saw this ordination platform (śīla-maṇḍala) and was filled with great joy, saying:
"All the monasteries in India possess such ordination platforms."

He further recounted the account of the Stone Precept Platform (Śīlā-maṇḍala) to the east of the kingdom of Udyāna; although the distance between the two is great, the ritual of the platform connects them.
As for the appearance of that platform, its lower two tiers are constructed by stacking stone courses, shaped like Mount Sumeru, with colored paths installed above and below.
On all four sides of the altar body, niches are arranged in rows, within which various spirit-kings (śrīdevaputra) are enshrined.
Upon both tiers of the foundation, stone balustrades are installed; beneath the pillars of these balustrades, lion-spirit-kings are positioned at intervals.

From atop the altar rise four tall stone pillars at each corner in two tiers; outside these pillars stand statues of the Four Heavenly Kings. Since they are situated in the open air, they are all carved from stone to ensure their long-term durability.

Upon the four-cornered railings, stone garuḍas are depicted with their mouths clutching dragons; this symbolizes that once a bhikṣu has received the precepts, he must constantly contemplate afflictions and karma in order to restrain and eliminate them.
The arrangement of divine images surrounding the ordination platform (*kṣetramaṇḍala*) symbolizes the aspect of long-lasting and firm protection.

These are the ceremonial insignia of the Great Sage and the expansive path for generating goodness. Although the diagrams have been fully displayed and their forms meticulously recorded, each possessing its own name and title, their significance is difficult to conceal. It is necessary to label their names and clearly exhibit their forms so that those who behold them may give rise to the aspiration for enlightenment and recognize the harmonious protection of both the unseen and the visible realms!
Now, according to the records:
Emperor Gaozu of the Liang dynasty commanded Shi Baocang to compose the *Shenguilü* (Records of Spirits and Ghosts), consisting of three fascicles in total.
Thus, its preface briefly states:

"Since the Tathāgata appeared in the world, his sublime teaching has been vast and far-reaching; there are no devas, nāgas, ghosts, or spirits who do not turn toward it. Thus, they are able to serve the Three Honored Ones and protect the fourfold assembly."

Generally, all spirits and deities have their respective abodes; thus, the deity who dwells upon the earth is named Sthāvarā (The Firm One). This extends even to temples, stupas, mountains, forests, rivers, seas, winds, and rains—as described in the *Dīrgha Āgama*—all of whom rely upon and guard the places they frequent. Now, regarding one side of this altar diagram, the three other sides are obscured and shadowed by various deities positioned at their flanks and backs, making it difficult to depict their forms.

In the illustrated manuals, the forms are arranged according to their respective directions—whether exposed or covered, standing or seated—and those who construct them later should place them in accordance with these scriptures.

Now, the names of the deities who protect the Buddha-stūpas listed above are mostly drawn from the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Abhiṣeka*, the *Mahāmāyūrī*, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, and other texts; because these sources contain extensive prose, they are here summarized collectively.
The deity named Vajrapāṇi (in the Liang language, "Vajra");
the deity named Balahaka (in the Liang language, "Wrestler"). First, the deity Resolute Radiance;

second, the deity Solar Radiance; third, the deity Sumeru Flower; fourth, the deity Pure Cloud Sound; fifth, the deity Asura King (taking the name of an asura, though he is not an asura); sixth, the deity Supreme Radiance; seventh, the deity Tree Sound; eighth, the deity Lion King—as explained above; ninth, the deity Thick Radiance Treasury; tenth, the deity Jewel Topknot Flower Light.
The above twelve Vajrapāṇi Śrī-rāja spirits are based on the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
The Vajra Spirits hold vajra-clubs, with fierce fires blazing intensely; it is also stated in the Sūtras and Vinaya:
"Eight Vajra Spirits stand in attendance at the four sides."
It is also said:
"Five hundred Vajrapāṇis constantly attend and protect the Buddha.
As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*:
"The various Vajra-devas, together with as many Malla-warriors as there are motes of dust, have long since made vows to attend upon the Tathāgata and uphold his bequeathed Dharma.

Now, according to the text, one seeks the characteristics [of the site], yet it does not mention a precept altar (śīlamaṇḍala); nevertheless, this precept altar is indeed a Buddha-stūpa, for it is where the śarīra is enshrined.
When sacred relics are interred within, how could they not be called a *stūpa*?
Those who are deluded by names and stubbornly cling to them need not be further evaluated.
To reiterate: as for the character "tǎ" (*stūpa*), in the local Chinese lexicons it is merely a word for an object; it was originally not a term from the Western lands [of India].
If following the Sanskrit manuscript, the place where the Buddha’s relics are enshrined is called "stūpa.
This is a contraction that omits the lower character "po" (婆) and pronounces only the upper character "ta" (塔).
Therefore, in the sūtras, it is sometimes called "stūpa," "sūtra-pa," and so forth.
According to the Chinese translation, "fāng-fén" (square mound), it refers to a tomb!
In ancient times, people buried their dead without raising mounds; a "mound" (fén) refers to the addition of earth upon the site.
As it says in the Vinaya:
"The Tathāgata knew that there were relics of Kāśyapa Buddha beneath the ground, and he increased the earth over them."
"This is precisely the form and appearance of a stūpa!

Now that the Buddha’s śarīra is enshrined within the ordination platform (sīmā-maṇḍala), its tiered foundation is distinguished, and divine images are arrayed in four directions to guard its manifest name—is this not indeed so?"
The twelve deities previously mentioned constantly guard the Buddha stupa.

Śākyamuni Tathāgata said:

The reason for taking the Buddha’s cubit as the standard of measurement is that the arm-bones of all Buddhas are composed of vajra; at the time of cremation, these arm-bones do not turn to ash, remaining as indestructible and solid śarīras that spread their transformative influence wherever they are located. Therefore, the dimensions of the altar and the body are determined by taking the Buddha’s cubit as the measure.
This is intended to cause the bhikṣus to maintain the precepts with a firmness like vajra, so that they remain unbroken.
The same applies to the *kṣetra-maṇḍala*: although it undergoes destruction at the end of an eon, it remains eternally present.
Measuring one cubit (*hasta*) of Śākyamuni Tathāgata corresponds to two cubits for an ordinary person; while the Tathāgata was in the world, he was twice the height of a human.

10. The Function and Scope of the Precept Platform (The Tenth Case on the Function and Scope of the Precept Platform). This is the site where the boundary is established; according to its limits, it extends downward to the wheel of the vajra, remaining indestructible even through the dissolution of kalpas.
As various treatises state, when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, the dharma of establishing boundaries (sīmā-bandha) is lost;
yet some commentators say that what was previously established is not lost, while subsequent establishments are not valid—this is the definitive conclusion.
Now, examining various traditions, it is evident that throughout India there are holy traces of the Buddha, all of which have endured through many kalpas and remain visible to this day.

Such things as the account of his self-sacrifice at the eight-lettered site, the signs of blood flowing from his children, the painful appearance of him breaking his bone to extract marrow, and the legacy of him spreading his hair to cover the mud—all these are solemnly established and manifest their traces as if at the very beginning.
Judging by these historical evidences, the realms and bonds of existence have not perished.
The Indian masters provide two interpretations of this.

The first states that the sacred signs of the consecrated boundary (*sīmā*) are all divine wonders, whereas calamities such as burning and flooding during the kalpa of destruction are mundane phenomena. Since mundane things are not the method for destroying the Path, the Dharma of the Path remains eternally present, causing these former signs to persist without interruption to this day.
A certain master of the treatises said:
"These are the traces of the Buddha's transformative manifestations; wherever they spread benefit, they shall ultimately never perish.
Therefore, when the three calamities arise, these sites sink along with the great earth into the void or the waters, their traces rarely to be found.

When the world is subsequently formed, all its existing locations re-establish themselves according to their former positions; therefore, it is not surprising that these sacred traces remain solemnly as they were at first!
Just as when the two realms of form and desire are both transformed into emptiness, and later established once more, they are set up exactly as they were placed before.

The karmic power of sentient beings is the first inconceivable thing; the Buddha’s transformative influence is the second inconceivable thing. How could the deliberations of ordinary people supersede the considerations of a Sage? Therefore, the established boundary remains firm and will certainly suffer no harm.
Question:

"If it is as you have described, and there are ancient traces of all four Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, with monasteries established and boundaries demarcated according to the constant practice of the Sangha, would establishing boundary markers now not result in overlapping with those ancient boundaries?"
"The re-binding has not been accomplished; the ritual procedure has failed!
How can this be resolved? He replied:
"Each follows the transformation of a particular Buddha; each is the Saṃgha of a particular Buddha. How could there be a son of the Benevolent One who takes Kāśyapa as his patron?
Since each takes their own teacher as their guide, they do not constitute a separate assembly."

For instance, throughout the lifetime of the Śākya-muni Buddha, the Saṃgha possessed the six points of harmony (*ṣaḍ-sāmagrī*); if even one person was discordant, they were not counted as a full number, and each formed their own distinct group based on their respective views and learning. Thus we know that the monastic boundaries (*saṃgha-dhātu*) of a preceding Buddha did not hinder the activities of a succeeding Buddha!
Therefore, in the *Lüchão* (Commentary on the Vinaya), it is stated that these five types of boundaries may be established concurrently without obstructing one another.

Furthermore, the foundations left by previous Buddhas are all utilized by subsequent Buddhas to establish their teachings; for instance, the site of Jetavana in Śrāvastī was a place where Buddhas have constantly traveled for ninety-one kalpas, and the story of Śāriputra feeling compassion upon seeing an anthill is well known.

Now, as for the dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom, they are the excellent fish-trap of all the sages;
the Vinaya and the Skillful Means of Birth are the guiding ferry across the three Buddhas' paths.
Thus we know that the precepts are the foundation for entering the state of sagehood and the basis for transcending the mundane world.
The Imperial Enlightenment relies upon this to manifest provisional means, and the True Dharma thereby abides for a long time.
Thus, when the Four Reliances govern the realm, they must take the Fundamental Precepts as the source from which wisdom springs;
and when the Five Vehicles are yoked together, they likewise rely on the Precepts as the primary means of spreading transformation.

Since the Dharma first flowed eastward and seven hundred years had passed, the platforms for the precept ordination (śīla-maṇḍala) have seen their names and realities diverge; those revealed in the Vinaya and Śāstras have spread as two distinct traditions, each prepared according to specific capacities and circumstances, being employed as the occasion demands.

In the Jin dynasty, there was the Ordination Platform at Nanlin Monastery in Yangzhou. When the virtuous armor-clad holy man first established its foundations, the distinction between the orthodox and the heterodox in the Central Plains had been silenced and forgotten; some took the great boundary as the ordination field, while others used a level clearing as the platform above.
This is because the Dharma was abolished three times and its later restoration depended upon the diligent efforts of those who held it fast;
or perhaps because teachers followed their own private judgments, severing scholarly discussion from the scriptural teachings.

As for the initial establishment of the *śīla-maṇḍala* and the exclusive propagation of the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, this truly stems from being encompassed by the Vinaya discipline, thereby employing it to unify both existence (*saṃsāra*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
In terms of its manifestation in sentient beings, it fills the great trichiliocosm; in terms of its discussion as a dharma, it encompasses all six stages.
Among the aggregates, bases, elements, and sense-fields, there is none that is not a condition for precepts;
from the supreme sages to the ordinary beings below, all rely upon the protection of the precepts.
Thus, the minor precepts and the major precepts reveal the beginning and end of the practice of conduct;
the presence or absence of vows manifests the gradual or sudden nature of the causal mind.
The Sūtra describes the aggregate of Bodhisattva precepts as not arising except through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal ritual of motion followed by three proclamations).
The Vinaya clarifies the authentic prohibitions for Śrāvakas, through which the fruit is realized by means of the tenfold Saṃgha;
if one wishes to perform these karmavācanās, one must rely upon the altar and the precincts, and thus it is named after the dharma of precepts, being entirely the foundation of pure conduct.

When the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) was first established, both the Sangha and the Dharma were instituted; yet when discussing the performance of formal acts (karmas), the boundary for the precept platform (śīla-maṇḍala) is more frequent. This is because the dwelling of the Sangha and the dwelling of the Dharma each have their own specific purpose.

Now, in establishing this site for the ordination platform, we have fully adhered to the instructions of the teachings: three markers are erected to demarcate two boundaries, and the open space is enclosed to eliminate confusion and doubt.

First, a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*) is established as the foundation of the site and platform; the assembly gathers according to natural circumstances, clarifying the distinct purposes of common and separate boundaries.

Third, the external characteristics of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept field) are described; by means of a formal motion and resolution (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), it is demarcated and bound. Thus, the three tiers stand solemnly and in alignment, with the steps for ascending and descending clearly defined;
the four corners are peaceful and situated in their respective places, marking the slant and correctness of the celestial hours.

Subsequently, the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) was demarcated and the monks emerged from the ordination platform (sīmaṇḍala). They gathered according to their respective locations and performed separate proclamations and separate bindings. This ensured that monastic affairs at the four sites would not fall into discord or division, allowing the virtues of the six harmonies to manifest and fulfilling the purpose of employing skillful means.
When their labors are accomplished, they do not perish for seventy thousand years;
when virtuous monks attain mastery, they do not vanish amidst the transformations of the three calamities.
From this it may be said that the establishment of the *śīma-kaṇḍa* (precept field) was not instituted in vain!
If it flourishes, the Buddha-dharma will abide forever;
if it decays, the true teaching will perish.
These words are not false; indeed, one must be all the more cautious!
Thus we know that the two precepts of restraint and discipline find their flourishing foundation in this stage;
likewise, the dual principles of upholding and violating are restored to purity through it.
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"If this precept did not exist, no wholesome dharmas would arise.
It is truly the fundamental basis of concentration and wisdom, and indeed the excellent medicine for karma and delusion!
Among contemporary practitioners, many treat it lightly; they do not establish the foundation of the altar, but rather transmit and receive [the teachings] according to mere convenience.
Some arbitrarily establish small boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*) when there is no difficult circumstance;
some occupy the Buddha hall while the monks all turn their backs on the image;
some wander in empty spaces, or stay in village quarters, becoming confused and separated from the assembly, thus chanting the texts in vain to perform the formal rite.
These matters are so complex and intermingled that they are not worth detailing!
Thus, the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* states:

"When monks from the Central Kingdom come wishing to receive the precepts, the procedures for the capital city are all carried out on boats upon the Yangtze River, where they form separate groups to receive them."
When asked the reason for this, he replied:

"The fundamental principles of the dharma of boundary-setting (sīmā-bandha) involve distinctions between common and separate boundaries that are difficult to discern. Therefore, while it is not difficult to maintain separation within a boat, it would be improper for rituals such as the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha) to fail to be accomplished."

Now, those who wish to uphold the True Dharma, propagate and protect the sacred rites, and sever the afflictions cannot attain liberation without the precepts; nor can they find a basis for their karma in the various stages and realms without the precepts.

Having vainly received the tonsure and robes, yet harboring no noble Dharma in one's heart, one merely wastes a lifetime and ultimately sinks into ten thousand kalpas; how could this not be a burden to oneself and others, and a hollow fulfillment of being a descendant of the World-Honored Śākyamuni?
Thus, those Brahman monks are so diligent, while these people of the cycle of birth and death are so indifferent; this is what the teachings of Mīti warn against—how can one not reflect upon it!
Someone who heard of this was startled and privately censured [the monks].

I told him: "It is not that I dare to establish something different; rather, this is precisely the same [truth]. The scriptures and teachings are complete and exhaustive; it is simply that people do not practice them.

I humbly consider that what the Pure Teaching elucidates takes reliance upon the Dharma as its foundation, clarifying the seals of the fourfold teaching and preserving the merit of the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka).
To comply with this is to raise the banner of the Triple Gem at the beginning of autumn; to violate it is to extinguish the legacy of the Fourfold Sangha.
The text states:
"The smallest boundary for the ordination platform (sīmā) shall accommodate twenty-one persons," which clarifies the maximum extent of the altar's dimensions.
"Reaching to where one can extend the hand" clarifies that the altar is not within a covered enclosure;
"leaving a space between" clarifies that the two boundaries are not directly joined;
"having first demarcated the site, the Great Boundary (mahā-sīmā) encircles it" clarifies the ritual procedure for the beginning and the end.
"Only establish the Buddha hall" clarifies that the Sangha Jewel is that upon which [the practice] relies;

"if there are monks residing there who possess shame and remove [defilements]" clarifies that when monks with a sense of shame propagate and uphold the precepts, their protection is easily accomplished.

In the past, there were masters who presided over the altar, yet the presence of monks upon the altar was not the constant practice of the site; this altar was intended solely for the maintenance of the precepts.
Nowadays, however, many monks reside there, which can certainly be understood in detail through the sincere teachings.

If these meanings were difficult to conceal or overlook, I have therefore set forth this formal account of its composition. With every task performed with utmost care and vigilance, I have collated and verified the text morning and night. Looking up to the entrusted legacy, I have provided thorough citations so that it may be perpetuated forever without obscurity. Thus it is said.

When darkness and ravines create obstacles and weary toil knows no rest, and these conditions persist for a long duration, from what can one derive a standard?

Therein lies one of brilliant attainment, renowned as a paragon among monks; his virtue flourishes as a hero of the age, and his wisdom encompasses the most eminent and heroic.
During the Qi and Liang dynasties, they fabricated [false] scriptures; both monastics and laypeople observed formal rites, establishing vast "Dharma fields" and arraying profuse ritual images.

Sublime indeed is the Perfectly Awakened One, who established the transformations of the Threefold World; the Precepts serve as the excellent guide, wherein all myriad virtues are expounded.
Colder than water and bluer than indigo—were it not for this organization, who else would find such things sweet?
The monastic community stands majestic like the great mountains and rivers, flourishing in its time; to build a merit altar is as if ascending the heights of a mountain.
The protection of the precepts leads one upward; both the realms of the unseen and the seen are traversed thereby. How vast is this legacy for future generations—it constitutes a sublime path!
I venture to recount these timely circumstances so that they may spread far and wide as a fragrant record.

Tracing back from the peaks of Mount Jing to seek the truth at Taiyi, the rarefied style of this age has been further propagated on this day.

The altar’s design follows the mountain’s contours, and the ascent and descent proceed with orderly ritual; enshrining the remains as a sacred relic, one’s profound sincerity is thus brought to completion.
May my aspirations reach far and wide, and may I be able to maintain reverence; may the mirror of consciousness be clear and bright, and the river of the mind be stilled of its waves.
Thus, as the kalpa-stone gradually wears away, I hope to behold the divine pearl within the wondrous form.

The Ritual for the Ordination Platform in the Central Plains and the Guanzhong Region of the Great Tang. On the eighth day of the second month in the second year of the Qianfeng era, I established the ordination platform. Monks from the four directions, mountains, and rivers, who gathered from afar upon hearing the news, numbered more than twenty.

By the beginning of summer, the assembly had gathered even more; they received the full precepts (*upasampadā*), most of whom were people from distant regions, while fellow students from the capital temples all came to observe their transformation.
I have long aspired to practice for the benefit of the Dharma, yet I fear there may be instances of discord;
my priority has been to ensure harmony between superiors and subordinates and to focus on the successful completion of the task.

There is Master Zhenyi of Ximing Monastery in the capital, who is a preeminent master of the Vinaya today. He is powerful and resolute, and I have always held him in high regard; however, I fear that if we were to turn eastward and circumambulate to the left, it would contravene the customary practices of the world.
I exhorted him, saying:
"Venerable Vinaya Master, do not regard this turning to the east and circumambulating to the left as contrary to the Dharma!
This is the great principle of the eternal order of Heaven."
"Human beings are deluded by what lies to their left and right, and long-standing customs rarely allow for discernment; I sincerely hope you will understand this and not worry about it being a fault.
He then replied to me, saying, "I do not dare find this strange."

"In the past, when I saw the Great Virtuous Master Gong of Dazhuangyan Monastery walking in meditation, he would invariably turn east and then turn north; this was his way of performing the circumambulation to the right (pradakṣiṇā).

He told me: 'Do you not see the city gates in the secular world? One enters from the east and exits from the west; everyone says that exiting to the left and entering from the right constitutes the proper direction.'"
Thus it is said, and so forth.
When practicing these rites, one observes the timing and regulations; if they are not considered pure in other regions, they are not practiced there.
Now that I am in my seventies, my feet are crippled and worn out, yet I do not consider the distance of mountains and passes when seeking those who would study the Dharma.

Now that the autumn air has grown clear, my guest’s heart soars with longing; as we are about to part for a separation that shall last until the end of days, the time for our next meeting will surely be delayed. Therefore, I have exerted myself despite my illness to assemble this, to serve as a parting gift for the final farewell.
It is said that these tears are shed because the destitute and solitary are pitiable.

On the fourteenth day of the second month in the second year of the Qiandeng era, at Qingguan, the Great Boundary was established as a pure ground, and an edict was issued for the purification of the kitchen.

The Scripture on the Diagrams for Establishing the Ordination Platform in Guanzhong: The Way of our Patriarch is like the rising sun ascending from the horizon; what thing would not be illuminated by it!

Fortunately, in my early years, I sought out teachers and inquired after the path, probing the depths of its profound principles. At that time, while serving as an administrative monk (jièdù sēng), I found the task of transmitting and expounding this Way to be difficult indeed.

I subsequently remained at Kaiyuan Zhaokong Temple, where I encountered Zen Master Zhengwu as my preceptor. We reconstructed the ordination platform (jietan), and I was honored to participate in the deliberation of its regulations.

As the platform was nearing completion, I reflected upon the *Jietan tu jing* (Diagram and Scripture of the Ordination Platform) by our patriarch; although Master Zhennu had once carved it into woodblocks, they were reduced to ashes by the fires of war. Fearing deeply that the Way might be lost, I mobilized my fellow practitioners to once again carve the original edition for circulation, so that it might endure forever and ensure that those of later generations would know the excellence of the platform’s design.
Composed on the first day of the twelfth month in the twenty-second year of the Shaoxing era by the bhikṣu Weiding, abbot of Wolong Jingde Monastery.
